title: Buying a Condo? What Lenders Look for Beyond Your Credit
description: Condo financing reviews the building and HOA, not just you. Learn about condo questionnaires, warrantable vs. non-warrantable projects, and HOA red flags.
keywords: buying a condo in Orange County
image_alt: A low-angle view of a high-rise residential building

faq.a: A warrantable condo is in a project that meets Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac guidelines for things like owner occupancy, budget reserves, litigation, and single-entity ownership.

faq.q: Can I get a loan on a non-warrantable condo?
faq.a: Yes, through portfolio or non-QM lenders, though terms usually differ from conventional financing.

faq.q: Does an FHA loan work for any condo?
faq.a: FHA loans generally require the condo project to be FHA-approved, though single-unit approvals are possible in some cases.

body_html:
Condos are often the most attainable path to ownership in coastal Southern California. They also come with an extra layer of underwriting many buyers don't expect: the lender reviews the building and the homeowners association, not just you.

Understanding that review early can save you from falling in love with a unit your loan can't finance.

Why the building matters

When you buy a condo, you share responsibility for the building with every other owner. If the HOA is underfunded, tied up in litigation, or dominated by investors, the risk to the lender increases. So lenders look at the health of the whole project.

Warrantable vs. non-warrantable

A "warrantable" condo meets Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac project guidelines and can be financed with conventional loans. A "non-warrantable" condo doesn't meet one or more of those standards. Common reasons include:

  • A high share of units owned by investors or rented out
  • One person or entity owning a large number of units
  • Pending litigation involving the HOA
  • Insufficient reserves in the HOA budget
  • A significant share of commercial space
  • Short-term rental or hotel-style operations

Non-warrantable doesn't mean unfinanceable. Portfolio and non-QM lenders regularly finance these units, often with different down payment and pricing expectations. As a broker, I can compare those options when a conventional loan won't fit.

The condo questionnaire

Early in escrow, your lender sends the HOA or its management company a questionnaire. It asks about owner occupancy, budget, reserves, delinquencies, litigation, and insurance. Management companies typically charge a fee and can take several days to respond, so ordering it promptly matters.

DocumentWhat it tells the lender
Condo questionnaireOccupancy, delinquencies, litigation, commercial space
HOA budgetWhether reserves are being funded adequately
Master insurance policyCoverage for the building and common areas
CC&Rs and bylawsRental restrictions and owner obligations

FHA and VA condos

For FHA financing, the project generally needs to be on HUD's approved list, though single-unit approvals are possible in some situations. VA keeps its own list of approved condo projects. If you're planning to use FHA or VA, check the project's status before you write an offer. If it isn't approved, a conventional loan may be the better route; see FHA vs. conventional for the trade-offs.

Insurance: two policies, not one

The HOA's master policy covers the building structure and common areas. You'll typically need your own "walls-in" policy, often called HO-6, to cover the interior of your unit and your belongings. Your lender will confirm both are in place before closing.

Smart questions to ask before you offer

  1. Has the project financed recently with conventional, FHA, or VA loans?
  2. Are there any special assessments planned or underway?
  3. Is there pending litigation?
  4. What's the rental cap, if any?
  5. How have HOA dues changed over the past few years?

How HOA dues affect what you can afford

HOA dues are part of your housing payment for qualification purposes. That means a condo with high dues can reduce the loan amount you qualify for, even if the purchase price is lower than a nearby single-family home. When comparing properties, look at the full monthly cost, not just the list price.

  • What dues usually cover: master insurance, exterior maintenance, common areas, some utilities, and contributions to reserves
  • What they may not cover: your interior insurance, utilities inside your unit, and special assessments
  • Why reserves matter: an HOA that funds reserves properly is less likely to hit owners with large special assessments later

If you're stretching to qualify, a unit with lower dues can make a meaningful difference. My guide to the debt-to-income ratio explains how the full payment flows into the calculation.

Red flags worth a second look

  1. A recent jump in dues without a clear explanation
  2. Minutes that mention deferred repairs, roof replacements, or structural studies
  3. Large numbers of owners behind on dues
  4. Insurance policies that have recently changed carriers or reduced coverage
  5. Ongoing disputes between the HOA and the developer or a contractor

None of these automatically kills a purchase. They're reasons to ask questions, read the documents carefully, and talk to your loan officer about whether the project will meet your lender's guidelines.

The takeaway

With a condo, you're qualifying the building as well as yourself. Ask about the project early, budget for HOA dues in your payment, and give your lender time to complete the review. Your agent and loan officer working together on this before you write an offer is the easiest way to avoid surprises.
